items.prose: A desk labels each daily close Below, Inside or Above a band around a stock's 20-day average. The labels follow the chain $P$ below, rows today and columns tomorrow.

parts.question: Today's close is Inside. What is the chance the close two days from now is Above? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take row Inside of $P$ times column Above of $P$.

byKey.squared: You squared the entry $0.1$. Two steps add every middle state: Inside then Above, or Above then Above.
byKey.one-path: That is the path through Inside alone. The close can also go Above at once and stay there: add $0.1 \times 0.6$.
byKey.one-step: That is tomorrow's chance. Two days need $P^2$.

explain.text: Split by tomorrow's label: Below then Above is impossible, Inside then Above gives $0.8 \times 0.1$, and Above then Above gives $0.1 \times 0.6$. In all $0.08 + 0.06 = 0.14$, entry (Inside, Above) of $P^2$.

parts.question: Write $\pi = (\pi_B, \pi_I, \pi_A)$ for the stationary distribution. Column Below of $\pi P = \pi$ gives $\pi_B = c\,\pi_I$. What is $c$? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write column Below: $0.5\pi_B + 0.1\pi_I + 0 \cdot \pi_A = \pi_B$, then solve for $\pi_B$.

byKey.inverted: You found $\pi_I = 5\pi_B$. The question asks for $\pi_B$ as a multiple of $\pi_I$.
byKey.no-move: You dropped the $0.5\pi_B$ on the left. Move it across: $0.5\pi_B = 0.1\pi_I$.
byKey.row: You used row Below, $(0.5, 0.5, 0)$, which adds to 1. $\pi P = \pi$ uses the columns of $P$.

explain.text: Column Below says the chance of Below tomorrow, $0.5\pi_B + 0.1\pi_I$, equals $\pi_B$. So $0.1\pi_I = 0.5\pi_B$ and $\pi_B = 0.2\pi_I$. Column Above gives $\pi_A = 0.25\pi_I$ in the same way.

parts.question: Using $\pi_B = 0.2\pi_I$ from part 2 and $\pi_A = 0.25\pi_I$ from column Above, what is $\pi_I$, the long-run share of Inside closes? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The three shares add to 1: $0.2\pi_I + \pi_I + 0.25\pi_I = 1$.

byKey.equal: Three labels do not mean three equal shares. Use the two ratios and the normalising equation.
byKey.stay: That is $P_{II}$, the chance an Inside close stays Inside. The share comes from $\pi P = \pi$.
byKey.no-move-carry: That uses $\pi_B = 0.1\pi_I$, the slip of dropping $0.5\pi_B$ in part 2. With 0.2 the share is $\tfrac{20}{29}$.
byKey.no-self: You left $\pi_I$ itself out of the sum, $\tfrac{1}{0.45}$. A share above 1 is a sign: add $\pi_I$.

explain.text: The normalising equation ties the scale: $\pi_I(0.2 + 1 + 0.25) = 1$. So $\pi = (\tfrac{4}{29}, \tfrac{20}{29}, \tfrac{5}{29}) \approx (0.138, 0.690, 0.172)$. Column Inside then holds by itself, a check.

parts.question: A trader takes $\pi \approx (0.138, 0.690, 0.172)$ from part 3. She uses it as the chances for the close 60 days ahead, whatever today's label. Is that sound?

options.text: Yes: every label reaches every other, and the self-loops rule out a period, so $\pi_0 P^k \to \pi$ from every start.
No: Below can only return to Below in an even number of days, so the chain is periodic.
options.why: Below has a self-loop of 0.5, so it can return in one day. No period locks its returns.

options.text: No: Below and Above cannot reach each other in one day, so the chain is reducible.
options.why: Reducible means some state can never reach another. Below reaches Above through Inside in two days.

options.text: No: $\pi$ is only the long-run share of days, never a chance for one day.
options.why: That holds for a periodic chain. This one is irreducible and aperiodic, so the chance itself converges.

feedback.correct: Correct. The chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so the theorem gives one $\pi$ that attracts every start.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check whether every label can reach every other, and whether returns are locked to a period.

explain.text: Each label reaches the others through Inside, so the chain is irreducible. Self-loops of 0.5, 0.8 and 0.6 rule out any period. So $\pi_0 P^{60}$ is close to $\pi$ whatever the start.

parts.question: A mean-reversion rule makes £3k on average on a day after a close outside the band. It loses £1k on average on a day after an Inside close. Using $\pi_I = \tfrac{20}{29}$, what is its long-run average P&L per day, in £k? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight each day's P&L by the long-run share of the close before it.

byKey.equal: You gave the three labels equal weight. Inside closes are $\tfrac{20}{29}$ of all days.
byKey.sign: You added the £1k. Days after an Inside close lose it.
byKey.stay: You used $0.8$ for the Inside share and $0.2$ for the rest. Use $\pi$ from part 3.
byKey.outside-only: That counts only the days after an outside close. Take off the £1k lost on the $\tfrac{20}{29}$ of days after an Inside close.

explain.text: Closes outside the band are $1 - \tfrac{20}{29} = \tfrac{9}{29}$ of days in the long run. So the average is $\tfrac{9}{29}(3) - \tfrac{20}{29}(1) = \tfrac{7}{29} \approx £0.24$k a day. The rule wins on rare days and loses a little on most.

items.prose: A fund trials a new strategy with small money, week by week. In Test it stays in Test with chance 0.5, goes live and On with chance 0.3, or is Shut with chance 0.2. A live strategy is On or Off each week: On stays On with chance 0.9, and Off returns to On with chance 0.4. Shut is for good.

parts.question: A strategy is in Test this week. What is the chance it is On two weeks from now? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Split by next week's state: Test then On, or On then On.

byKey.test-test: That is Test, Test, On alone. It can also go On at once and stay On: add $0.3 \times 0.9$.
byKey.on-on: That is the path through On alone. It can also wait a week in Test: add $0.5 \times 0.3$.
byKey.squared: You squared the entry 0.3. Two steps add every middle state.

explain.text: Row Test of $P$ is $(0.5, 0.3, 0, 0.2)$ and column On is $(0.3, 0.9, 0.4, 0)$. Their product is $0.15 + 0.27 = 0.42$, entry (Test, On) of $P^2$.

parts.question: Once live, the strategy moves only between On and Off. In the long run, what share of live weeks is it On? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.correct: Flow out of On, $0.1\pi_{\text{On}}$, equals flow in, $0.4\pi_{\text{Off}}$, so $\pi_{\text{On}} = \tfrac{0.4}{0.1 + 0.4} = 0.8$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Balance the flow out of On against the flow into On, with the two shares adding to 1.

byKey.stay: That is $P_{\text{On,On}}$. The long-run share comes from $\pi P = \pi$ on the live class.
byKey.swapped: That is the Off share. On is left less often, so it holds more of the time.
byKey.equal: On and Off are not equally sticky. Balance $0.1\pi_{\text{On}} = 0.4\pi_{\text{Off}}$.
byKey.stay-ratio: That is $\tfrac{0.9}{0.9 + 0.4}$. Use the chances of leaving: $\tfrac{0.4}{0.1 + 0.4}$.

explain.text: On and Off form a closed class with its own stationary distribution. Column On gives $0.1\pi_{\text{On}} = 0.4\pi_{\text{Off}}$, so $\pi_{\text{On}} = 4\pi_{\text{Off}}$ and $(\pi_{\text{On}}, \pi_{\text{Off}}) = (0.8, 0.2)$.

parts.question: Shut takes the strategies that never go live. What is the chance a strategy in Test ever goes live? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Condition on the first week: live at once, or still in Test and starting afresh.

byKey.one-week: That is next week alone. A strategy still in Test gets another chance each week.
byKey.two-weeks: That stops after two weeks, $0.3 + 0.5 \times 0.3$. Solve $h = 0.3 + 0.5h$ for every week.
byKey.carry: That is the chance of being On in two weeks. Going live needs no particular week, and Off weeks count too.
byKey.total: You added the 0.5 of staying in Test to the 0.3. Staying is not going live: it only starts the wait again.

explain.text: From Test the chain leaves for live with chance 0.3 or for Shut with 0.2 each week. First-step analysis gives $h = 0.3 + 0.5h$, so $h = 0.6$: of the weeks that end the trial, 3 in 5 send it live.

parts.question: Use $h = 0.6$ from part 3 and the On share $0.8$ from part 2. What is the chance that a strategy in Test today is On in a week far ahead? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The limit mixes the live class and Shut, weighted by the chance of ending in each.

byKey.ignores-shut: That is the answer for a strategy already live. From Test it is Shut for good with chance 0.4.
byKey.live-only: That is the chance it is live at all. Live strategies are On only $0.8$ of the time.
byKey.two-step: That is two weeks ahead, from part 1. Far ahead the chance settles elsewhere.
byKey.whole-chain: That assumes Shut takes all the long-run chance, as a lone absorbing state would. The live class is closed too and keeps 0.6 of it.

explain.text: The chain is reducible: it ends in the live class with chance 0.6, or in Shut with 0.4. Inside the live class it settles at $(0.8, 0.2)$. So the limit for On is $0.6 \times 0.8 = 0.48$, and it depends on the start.

items.prose: A dealer answers a client's request for a quote. Each round the client trades, walks away or haggles. From a fresh Quote the client trades with chance 0.4, counters with chance 0.4 and walks with chance 0.2. After a Counter the dealer re-quotes with chance 0.5; otherwise the client trades with chance 0.2 or walks with chance 0.3.

parts.question: Let $q$ be the chance that a request at Quote ends in a trade. Write $h_C$, the chance from Counter, in terms of $q$.

feedback.correct: One round from Counter: trade at once with 0.2, or back to Quote with 0.5. So $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Condition on the next round from Counter and add the routes that end in a trade.

byKey.no-direct: You left out the client who trades straight after countering, with chance 0.2.
byKey.walk: You used the walk chance, 0.3. The routes to a trade are 0.2 at once and 0.5 back to Quote.
byKey.plus-one: There is no $+1$ here. That counts a round; a chance averages over where the round lands.

explain.text: From Counter the next round goes to Trade (0.2), Walk (0.3) or a fresh Quote (0.5). A fresh Quote then trades with chance $q$. Walk adds nothing, so $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$.

parts.question: Using $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$ from part 1, what is $q$, the chance a fresh quote ends in a trade? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $q = 0.4 + 0.4h_C$, put in part 1's $h_C$, and solve for $q$.

byKey.direct: That is a trade in the first round only. A counter can still lead to a trade.
byKey.one-pass: You stopped at $0.4 + 0.4 \times 0.2 = 0.48$. The re-quote starts afresh, so keep the $0.2q$ and solve.
byKey.no-direct: That uses $h_C = 0.5q$ from leaving out the direct trade after a counter. With $0.2 + 0.5q$, $q = 0.6$.
byKey.walk: That uses $h_C = 0.3 + 0.5q$, the walk chance in place of the trade chance. Use 0.2.

explain.text: First-step analysis from Quote gives $q = 0.4 + 0.4h_C$. With $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$ this is $0.8q = 0.48$, so $q = 0.6$ and $h_C = 0.5$. Row Quote of $(I - Q)^{-1}R$ says the same: $(0.6, 0.4)$.

parts.question: Let $t_Q$ and $t_C$ be the expected rounds until a request ends, from Quote and from Counter. Then $t_C = 1 + 0.5t_Q$. What is $t_Q$? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $t_Q = 1 + 0.4t_C$, put in $t_C = 1 + 0.5t_Q$, and solve.

byKey.one-pass: You stopped at $1 + 0.4 \times 1$. A re-quote starts the count again, so keep the $0.2t_Q$ and solve.
byKey.no-one: Without the $+1$ for each round, $t = 0$ solves the system. Every round counts one.
byKey.geometric: That is $\tfrac{1}{0.6}$, as if every round ended with Quote's chance 0.6. A round from Counter ends only with chance 0.5.
byKey.counter: That is $t_C = 1 + 0.5 \times 1.75$. The question asks for $t_Q$.

explain.text: Each round counts 1, then the request starts afresh where it lands: $t_Q = 1 + 0.4t_C$ and $t_C = 1 + 0.5t_Q$. So $0.8t_Q = 1.4$, giving $t_Q = 1.75$ rounds and $t_C = 1.875$.

parts.question: Part 2 found $q = 0.6$. With a tighter quote, a fresh quote trades with chance 0.5, counters with 0.3 and walks with 0.2. The Counter row is unchanged. What is the new $q$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Redo part 2 with the new Quote row: $q = 0.5 + 0.3h_C$ and $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$.

byKey.one-pass: You stopped at $0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.2$. Keep the $0.15q$ from the re-quote and solve.
byKey.old-hc: You used the old $h_C = 0.5$. It depends on $q$, which has changed: $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$.
byKey.direct: That is a trade in the first round only. Counters still lead to some trades.
byKey.old-q: That is the old quote's chance. The new Quote row changes the equations.

explain.text: Only the Quote row changes, so $q = 0.5 + 0.3h_C$ with $h_C = 0.2 + 0.5q$. That gives $0.85q = 0.56$ and $q \approx 0.6588$. The tighter quote wins about 6 more requests in 100.

parts.question: The dealer earns £50 a trade at the old quote and £40 a trade at the tighter one. Using $q = 0.6$ and $q \approx 0.6588$, which quote earns more per request, on average?

options.text: The old quote: about £30 a request, against about £26.35.
The tighter quote: it trades more often, so it earns more.
options.why: It trades more often, but $0.6588 \times 40 \approx 26.35$ is below $0.6 \times 50 = 30$.

options.text: They earn the same, since both quotes walk with chance 0.2 in the first round.
options.why: The walk chance in round one is the same, but the trade chances and the margins differ.

options.text: The tighter quote, because it ends requests in fewer rounds.
options.why: Rounds cost nothing here. Compare the expected margin per request, $q$ times the margin.

feedback.correct: Correct. Per request the old quote earns $0.6 \times 50 = £30$ and the tighter one $0.6588 \times 40 \approx £26.35$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each quote's chance of a trade by its margin.

explain.text: Expected margin per request is the chance of a trade times the margin. The old quote gives $0.6 \times 50 = 30$, the tighter one $0.6588 \times 40 \approx 26.35$. The extra trades do not make up for the lower margin.

items.prose: A takeover of a company is Announced. Each month an announced deal stays Announced with chance 0.5, moves to regulatory Review with chance 0.3, completes with chance 0.1 or is withdrawn with chance 0.1. A deal in Review stays in Review with chance 0.6, completes with chance 0.25 or is withdrawn with chance 0.15. A share is worth £10 if the deal completes and £6 if it is withdrawn.

parts.question: What is $h_R$, the chance a deal in Review completes? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Condition on the next month: complete at once, or stay in Review and start afresh.

byKey.one-month: That is next month alone. A deal still in Review gets another chance every month.
byKey.over-stay: You divided 0.25 by 0.6, the chance of staying. Divide by the chance of leaving Review, 0.4.
byKey.leave: That is the chance of leaving Review in a month, $0.25 + 0.15$. Of those exits, 0.25 in 0.4 are completions.

explain.text: First-step analysis gives $h_R = 0.25 + 0.6h_R$, so $0.4h_R = 0.25$. Of the months that end a review, 0.25 in 0.4 complete the deal: $h_R = 0.625$.

parts.question: Using $h_R = 0.625$ from part 1, what is $h_A$, the chance an announced deal completes? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $h_A = 0.1 + 0.5h_A + 0.3h_R$, then collect the $h_A$ terms.

byKey.no-loop: You left out the month that stays Announced: $0.1 + 0.3 \times 0.625 = 0.2875$. Add $0.5h_A$ and solve.
byKey.direct: That adds 0.1 and 0.3, as if every deal in Review completed and no month stayed Announced. Review completes with chance 0.625.
byKey.loop-once: You let the Announced loop run only once, $0.2875 \times 1.5$. Solve $h_A = 0.2875 + 0.5h_A$ for every month.

explain.text: One month from Announced: complete (0.1), stay (0.5) or move to Review (0.3), which completes with chance 0.625. So $h_A = 0.1 + 0.5h_A + 0.1875$, and $h_A = \tfrac{0.2875}{0.5} = 0.575$.

parts.question: A deal in Review is resolved in $t_R = \tfrac{1}{0.4} = 2.5$ months on average. What is $t_A$, the expected months until an announced deal is resolved? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count one month, then average where the deal lands: $t_A = 1 + 0.5t_A + 0.3t_R$.

byKey.no-loop: You left out the $0.5t_A$ for a month that stays Announced. Keep it and solve.
byKey.no-review: That is $\tfrac{1}{0.5}$, the time to leave Announced. A deal sent to Review still has 2.5 months to run.
byKey.no-one: You dropped the $+1$ for the month itself. Every month counts one.
byKey.added: You added the whole 2.5 months of Review to 2. Only the 0.3 of deals that go to Review spend it.

explain.text: First-step analysis: $t_A = 1 + 0.5t_A + 0.3t_R$, with $t = 0$ at Completed and Withdrawn. With $t_R = 2.5$ this is $0.5t_A = 1.75$, so $t_A = 3.5$ months.

parts.question: Using $h_A = 0.575$ from part 2, what is the expected value of a share when the deal is resolved, in pounds? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weight £10 by the chance of completion and £6 by the chance of withdrawal.

byKey.review-h: You used $h_R = 0.625$. The deal is Announced, so it completes with chance 0.575.
byKey.even: That gives the two outcomes equal weight. Completion has chance 0.575.
byKey.no-withdraw: You left out the £6 a share is still worth if the deal is withdrawn.
byKey.swapped: You gave 0.575 to the £6 outcome. Completion pays £10.

explain.text: Every deal is resolved, completed with chance 0.575 or withdrawn with chance 0.425. So the share is worth $0.575(10) + 0.425(6) = £8.30$ on average at the end.

parts.question: Holding a share costs £0.02 a month until the deal is resolved. Use £8.30 from part 4 and $t_A = 3.5$ months from part 3. What is the highest price today at which buying has a positive expected profit? Give your answer in pounds to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the expected holding cost, £0.02 times the expected months, off the expected value.

byKey.no-cost: That ignores the holding cost. The share is held 3.5 months on average.
byKey.review-time: You used $t_R = 2.5$ months. The deal is Announced, so it runs 3.5 months on average.
byKey.one-month: You charged one month. The cost runs every month until the deal is resolved.
byKey.carry-added: That uses 4.5 months, from adding all 2.5 months of Review to 2. Only the 0.3 of deals sent to Review spend them: 3.5 months.

explain.text: Expected profit is $8.30 - \text{price} - 0.02 \times E[T]$, and $E[T] = 3.5$. It is positive while the price is below $8.30 - 0.07 = £8.23$. The cost uses the expected time because the monthly cost adds up over the months held.
